question.text: A ratchet / anti-dilution clause in an AIF investment agreement primarily protects the AIF investor against:

answer.text: A subsequent funding round done at a higher valuation than the AIF's entry price
A subsequent funding round done at a lower valuation (a 'down round'), by adjusting the AIF's economics to offset the dilution
A fall in listed-equity prices on the stock exchange after the investment
A change in the management team of the investee company

explanation.text: The Logic: A ratchet / anti-dilution clause protects the AIF investor when the investee company raises a future round at a price lower than the AIF's original entry price. The workbook describes this as a mechanism that may provide additional shares to the AIF to offset the dilution caused by the cheaper share issuance. The Trap: Anti-dilution does not protect against all dilution — issuing more shares at a higher valuation is not penalised. It is specifically a down-round protection, and it is unrelated to listed market price movements or management changes. Note: Rewritten as a generic down-round / ratchet protection item, because the checked workbook does not define "full ratchet" mechanics (price reset to the new lower round price) in the specific terms used in the original explanation.
